newsitem.title: CUBA: Santa Claus skips Cuba, at least officially.
newsitem.headline: Santa Claus skips Cuba, at least officially.

text.p: While it is hardly consumer hysteria, Cubans spend small fortunes on plastic Christmas trees and decorations and try to put together special dinners in their homes on Christmas Eve.
But for the government, Dec. 24 and 25 are just ordinary working days and Christmas is a low-key affair.

As in most Communist-ruled nations, the seasonal public holiday is New Year's Day, also the anniversary of the day President Fidel Castro and his guerrilla army overthrew dictator Fulgencio Batista in 1959.
The Christmas holiday was cancelled in Cuba in 1969 -- the year the island was striving for a sugar cane harvest of 10 million metric tons -- and has not been restored.

This year the National Assembly is holding its sole two-day annual session on Dec. 24 and 25. Parliament normally sits later in the month, around Dec. 26 to 29. The timing has raised eyebrows among foreign observers, some of whom expected a nod to Christmas amid current efforts by Cuban authorities to ease relations with the Roman Catholic church.
Castro held a historic first meeting with Pope John Paul II at the Vatican last month and it was agreed the pontiff will visit the Caribbean island next year.

But authorities have shrugged off any suggestion that the timing of the parliamentary session is unusual. Foreign Ministry spokesman Miguel Alfonso, asked about the dates, reminded reporters these are ordinary working days in Cuba.

Cubans, including state firms, send cards at this time of the year, with a "Happy New Year" message. But for those who can afford them, small plastic Christmas trees sold in hard currency stores are popular. The hard currency stores also sell seasonal hampers of wine and packs of "turron," Spanish candy, although the prices are prohibitive for most Cubans.
Despite lean economic times, many Cubans, especially Christians, also try to assemble a traditional Christmas Eve dinner, usually of pork or fish with rice and beans.

Last year authorities clamped down on Christmas trees after they started to appear in public places. Communist Party leaders reminded state enterprises and other state institutions such as hospitals they were not allowed to put up trees.

The Christmas period also coincides with the start of the main tourist season in Cuba. Hotels, restaurants and some state hard currency stores display trees and other seasonal ornaments. But there are no decorations to be seen on the streets.

Foreign vistors doing Christmas shopping in the city's hard currency stores find the experience a refreshing, or depressing, contrast to the consumer frenzy at home. There are lines to deposit bags or packages before entering and a policy, also to prevent shoplifting, of locking the doors and allowing only three or four customers in the stores at a time.
